utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Mr. Hamdija Vilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may sit and you may begin, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you to begin by telling us your full name?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: My name is Hamdija Vilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: The 31st of March, 1957.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where did you live prior to the outbreak of the conflict in 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I lived in the village of Prelovo, Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Have you ever been convicted of a crime?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What crime have you been convicted of?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Murder in self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When were you convicted of that crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you serve a jail sentence after your conviction for that crime?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was a five-year prison sentence and I served that in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, you haven't requested any protected measures but some persons that I believe you may mention during your testimony are the subject of protective measures. So to facilitate your evidence here today I'm going to ask that you be shown a pseudonym sheet, I note I provided copies to both Defence teams prior to the start of the session. I'm going to ask that you read it. I'm going to ask that you not say the names out loud, but simply after reading it, tell us do you know the people who are named on that sheet?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And during the course of your testimony, I would ask that you refer to those persons by the pseudonyms that are -- that have been assigned by the Chamber, namely, MLD-2 and MLD-10. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if you need to refer to a person MLD-10's husband, I ask that you refer to him as that, the husband of MLD-10. I'd ask you now put your initials on that document, and ask that it be shown to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After the Chamber has seen it, I would ask that it be tendered into evidence. Your Honours, I have three additional copies for the Chamber as it might facilitate your efforts to follow the testimony as its given. They are simply photocopies of the exhibit so the Chamber can have them before them as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit P149, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, just one additional question regarding your conviction. Can you tell us the circumstances surrounding the event after which you were convicted?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: It was in a bar in Visoko, and I acted in self-defence. It was a brawl including some drunken persons and the waitress.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you use a weapon during the course of that event?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: A hand grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you, did you serve in the military?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When did you first serve in the military?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: In 1976. It was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long was your military service which commenced in 1976?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: 15 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you also serve in the military at a later point in your life?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: As of the 20th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how long was your military service this time?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Drawing your attention now to June of 1992, at that time did you have a brother who lived in the Visegrad area known as Bikavac?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, Hasan Vilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you moved your family to your brother's house?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Between the 5th and 8th of June, 1992, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you staying at that house at that time as well?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, for about ten days or so, and I was also hiding in the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you say you were hiding in the forest, where in relation to Bikavac was this forest?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: The settlement is called Ban Polje, just above the settlement of Bikavac. To the right of my brother's house there are two groves and that is where I hid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever come a time when you saw a soldier you recognised come to that house?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, pursuant to the decision of this honourable Trial Chamber from the 6th of November, the examination of this witness is restricted just to the matter arising out of the Defence alibi of Milan Lukic. So by these questions I think that my learned friend from OTP is spreading matters for examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's perfectly true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I just might explain. In one question in a non-leading way I'm just trying to establish that he knows Milan Lukic. If I'm permitted to ask a leading question on that, then we don't need that particular question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you summarize how you know him?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: My aunt lived in Rujiste and he and his cousin Sredoje Lukic lived there. I frequently visited the place. Otherwise, I occasionally saw him on the bus in town. I also know Sredoje Lukic because he used to be a policeman. I know him better than I do Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with a fire in Bikavac in which a large number of civilians perished?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, relevance beyond the scope of alibi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this man believes the reason he was approached by the Defence to give this evidence was that it would be believed because he lost his wife and three children in Bikavac, I'm just asking him now to establish who the victims are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a fire in Bikavac in which a large number of civilians perished?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When do you believe it occurred?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection. It calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Either he knows or he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, do you know when the fire occurred?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: On the 27th of June, that is to say, between the 27th and the 28th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you personally witness it?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you related to any of the victims?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Just a minute. Let's hear Mr. Cepic first.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise for this interruption. Page 11, line 10, we haven't got an answer in transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Yes. What was your answer, witness, when you were asked did you personally witness it? "It" being the fire. What answer did you give?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not witness it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And Your Honour, again we would object that this is beyond the scope of alibi rebuttal, any questions regarding Bikavac, also the witness does not have a specific personal knowledge as to whom died in what fire and when, and in fact, I don't believe the witness Zehra Turjacanin identified his family as the victims. I do note the indictment has some persons with the same last name as this witness indicted but it also says 70 people died in the Bikavac fire, and the Bikavac indictment only names a few people, much less than 70. So I would argue that everything about this questioning calls for speculation and is otherwise improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interruption. Again we haven't got answer in transcript. Line 19, page 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Line?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Line 19. Probably technical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Well, I can tell you, the witness said he was not personally acquainted with the fire. He did not see it. Isn't that so, Mr.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, are you coming to the core of the questioning? Because it's being said that you are going outside the scope of what you are permitted by the Chamber to lead?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm doing my best to keep it as narrow as possible. The objection is that I haven't laid a basis for how he know that his family was killed in the fire; I can certainly do that. I thought that would be beyond the scope that the Chamber had permitted me. But it's clearly his belief that he was approached simply because no one would ever believe that a man who lost his family in a fire would then appear as an alibi witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us who, if anyone, that was related to you, you believe perished in the Bikavac fire on the 27th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was my wife, Mina Vilic, who was born in 1955. My daughter, Nihada Vilic, born in 1981. My other daughter, Zihneta Vilic, born in 1984. And my son, Nihad Vilic, born in 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we now go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vilic, prior to start of this trial, had you had any contact with the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Drawing your attention to June of this year, did you receive a phone call related to this case?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Around the 4th. It may have been the 5th of June, I do not recall exactly. I received a phone call from MLD-10's husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you recall the substance of what was said during that phone call?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: The substance of it was in that MLD-10's husband asked me if he could ask some questions of me, which may be painful, but may turn out to be good for me. I asked him, well, what do you mean specifically? Whereupon he said that he was in contact with Milan Lukic. Milan Lukic asked him to speak to me, asking if I could provide my telephone number to Milan Lukic in order for Milan to get in touch with me from The Hague. I thought about it for a moment, whether to do it or not, and I said that I agreed to it. I told him to give him my telephone number so that he could call.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he say anything with respect to MLD-10 herself, and her role in this?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: MLD-10 and her husband told me that I was supposed to give a statement on Mr. Milan Lukic's behalf, and that he would provide me with everything I might need in life, including assets. I was curious after hearing that, and I agreed to talk to Milan Lukic, and so it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During this phone call, were you given any instructions with respect to how matters would proceed?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What were they?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I was told that some of his people would call me. In any case, they never did. I was also told that all things were supposed to go via MLD-10's husband and herself, that all information was to arrive that way. They were supposed to tell me what to do, how, and when.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you given any instructions with respect to how to conduct yourself during a phone conversation if Milan Lukic called?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What instructions were you given?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I was told that Milan Lukic would call and that his ID, his number would be withheld. You would not be able to see it on your mobile screen. You will know immediately that it is Milan Lukic calling. Do not mention any war events or any victims because his conversations from the detention unit in The Hague are being recorded and that could be to the detriment of his Defence. I agreed to it, not to mention those topics. Subsequently when we talked on the phone, I did not mention such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Why did you agree to engage in a phone conversation with Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I wanted to see what Mr. Milan Lukic wanted from me. I know he burnt my family alive and destroyed my life. I wanted know what it was that he wanted from me. That was my only reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you received a second phone call related to this case?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, there did. There was a second phone call from The Hague from Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When was that phone call?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: That phone call was on the 8th of June, 2008. I can't say precisely at what time, but in any case between 3.00 and 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did the person who called you at that time introduce themselves by name?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes. On my mobile telephone screen I saw that the number was withheld. The person calling introduced himself as Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you summarize as best you are able what, if anything, was said to you during that phone call.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: He introduced himself saying that he was Milan Lukic. He asked me, How are you Mr. Vilic, sir? I said I was all right. He asked me how I was and how my life is. I asked him, well, I get by. Then he said that some of his people would arrive and that we are to engage in negotiations via MLD-10. He instructed me to address her as his sister. He said that his people would arrive and that we were to arrange on the course of the future work. I accepted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Approximately how long was that phone conversation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: 5 or 6 minutes, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there a third phone call that you received related to this case?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There was a third phone call from MLD-10's husband and herself. I believe it was on the 19th of June, 2008. They said that they had talked to Milan Lukic and his attorneys. They told me that I was supposed to go to Zavidovici to their house. They also told me that the attorneys were supposed to be there on the 22nd of June, 2008. To MLD-10's husband's house, that is the place where they live. I asked him how I was supposed to get to Zavidovici. MLD-10's husband told me, Take the most expensive taxi you can get from Sarajevo, you will be reimbursed for everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did they give you a specific time that they wanted you to come to their house?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Around 12.00. However, I went a bit earlier. It was during the summer and it was hot --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before we --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: -- I left around 6.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before we move from this phone call, I wanted to ask you a few more specific questions. What was your response to this request to come to their home on the 22nd of June?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: My response, after I was instructed to take a taxi, was that I would be there in the house to meet the attorneys.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Approximately how long was this phone call?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Well, this particular one may have lasted for about 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you receive a fourth phone call related to this case?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received a fourth call from Mr. Milan Lukic from The Hague. The number was withheld. He introduced himself as Milan Lukic again. He asked me whether I had received information that his people are to visit MLD-10's sister's home on the 22nd of June at 12.00. I answered yes. And I told him that I had received that call, and that I would be going to meet them, to get to that appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, so the record is clear, the first call that you received from a person who identified themselves as Milan Lukic, was that call to the phone number that you gave us in private session?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This phone call that you are now describing, was it also made to that same phone number?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: On the same number, yes. On the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long did this phone conversation last, this fourth phone call related to the case?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: He phoned on the 21st of June at 1510, lasted not even two minutes. The conversation was disconnected, and in two minutes' time, he phoned again around 1512. And then we talked about the meeting which I already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he explain to you what would occur during that meeting the next day?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: No. Milan did not want to explain things because everything was being recorded, and he said that his people would explain everything to me, together with MLD-10, his sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you go to where you were asked to go to for this meeting?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I got up on the 22nd of June. I had my coffee. I got up early, around 6.00 a.m., because it was summer, very high temperatures, so I wanted to arrive there before it got too hot. I found MLD-10 and her husband at their home. They were sitting and having coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, if I could just ask you some specific questions. What time do you recall arriving at the home of MLD-10?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Somewhere around 8.30, 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who was present in the house when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: MLD-10's husband and MLD-10 herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened -- did you go inside the house?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened inside the house?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: They offered me some coffee. I said I did not want any because I had had one coffee in Sarajevo already. He offered me a beer and I accepted. We drank beer and talked. MLD-10 produced a sheet of paper like this one, written on both sides, something was written on it. On the first page, it was addressed to me and the other was addressed to MLD-10 sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, again if I could ask you some specific questions. The piece of paper that you are referring to now, was it hand written or was it typed?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Hand written, in Cyrillic alphabet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did MLD-10 tell you what this piece of paper was before she gave it to you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. MLD-10 told me, here, Milan wrote down what I should answer on behalf of his Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you allowed to read what was on the back of the piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: No. MLD-10 would not allow me to read that. She said that Milan Lukic had addressed that to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, as precisely as you are able, can you tell us what was contained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. You said that MLD-10 would not allow you to read what was on the back. Did you specifically ask her or indicate to her that you wanted to read what was on the back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. But she said, It's of no interest to you, this is mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vilic, could I ask you as precisely as you are able to tell us what you recall about what was on the portion of that letter addressed to you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. What was written was this: Sir, Mr. Hamdija Vilic, you will say as follows, that I, Hamdija Vilic, military commander of the Muslim forces intercepted a Serb military column of vehicles in the village of Kopito above Visegrad, killed three Serbian officers, and they provided me with some names, but I did not memorize them. I had no need to do so. And that I kept Milan Lukic and his army for three days and three nights encircled, to be more precise from the 13th of June, 1992, to 15th of June, 1992. And that he could not have been during those three days in the town of Visegrad. And that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did the letter refer to anything with respect to Milan Lukic's character?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: In connection with the character? I did not understand your question quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall it saying anything about Milan Lukic generally?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Not about his character. The narrative was that I had him and his army encircled, this is the only thing that was referred to in that letter, that he could not have broken out of encirclement because of the Muslim forces, and that he was stuck there for three days in the forest, and that he could not have managed to reach the town of Visegrad during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did this letter make any reference to your wife and children?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: No, no. No. Milan had told me that I would be finding out the truth about my wife, children, brother, neighbours, that I would finally get to know the whole truth about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: During a telephone conversation, I forgot to mention that earlier. This was during a telephone conversation when he called me from The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've made reference to two telephone conversations you believe you had --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, two, two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall whether it was in the first one or in the second one that he told you you would find out information --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: During the second one. During the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After you read the letter, what happened?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: We continued sitting in that house. It was a nice sunny day. We sat in the garden. We awaited the lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could we just follow-up on the conversation between Milan and himself when Milan told him that he would find out about members of his family. Did you follow up on that? Did you ask him anything in relation to that? For example, how you would find out about your family members? In other words, was there anything more to that conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he said that I would be finding the entire truth probably about my family, my brother and everybody else when I get to testify about him. He did not want to be -- put it more precisely as to where, when, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you say anything to him in response to that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, drawing your attention back to the period of time when you are waiting with MLD-10 and her husband, was there ever any conversation related to this case?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did talk a little bit about that with MLD-10 and her husband, about how he would be providing me with everything that I would need in life, including money.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there ever a discussion about MLD-2?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes. MLD-2, MLD-10 told me that, but also the MLD-2 because we are, after all, relatives. He received 5.000 Euro from Mr. Milan Lukic. I don't know through which channels he managed to do so, neither am I interested in that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The transcript has terminated. May I ask that that be checked into by the technical personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have -- it seems that, if this assists, that the LiveNote version from my computer has stopped, but I still have the full transcript on my screen, I'm not sure what it's called but the LiveNote version that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can continue then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, we had the -- we experienced a problem when you were in the middle of an answer. So can I ask you to repeat, what was the discussion with respect to MLD-2? Can you summarize that for us.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I know MLD-2 well, as well as I know MLD-10. They are brother and sister. Siblings. MLD-10 told me then how she had taken 5.000 Euro to MLD-2 to the place of Ilijas, and that she had given him those 5.000 Euros which had been sent by Milan Lukic so that he could pay for the house bought at Ilijas. So that MLD-2 would confirm what Milan Lukic was asking me to confirm, but since MLD-2 was not in the territory of Visegrad in 1992 until the end of the war in 1996, he was in the area between Zepa and Srebrenica. And so MLD-2, he is prone to excessive drinking, he had spent the money that he received. He did not pay for the house, and he refused to come to testify, of course, since he knew nothing. And whomever calls his mobile -- so whenever somebody calls his mobile, he does not dare to answer the phone, not even my calls. And this is what specifically said MLD-10 to me, and MLD-2 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can I ask you, did there come a time when other people came to the house of MLD-10? If I can ask you just to give me a short answer and I'll ask you specific questions about this.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall the time that other people came to the house?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Around 1.30 p.m., thereabouts. 1330.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many people came to the house?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to describe them in brief terms, and then I will ask you some specific questions about each one individually.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: One was some 191 or 192 centimetres tall, nicely dressed, well shaven, brown-black hair, short hair. One was shorter, maybe 180, 182 centimetres, tall, clean shaven, short hair. They came to that house, the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did they introduce themselves?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but I did not memorize their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did they indicate where they were from?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes. The taller one said he was from Belgrade, Serbia; and the other one said that he was from America.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. You've given us a description of someone already as being 191, 192 centimetres tall. Was that the person who identified himself as being from Serbia or the person who identified himself as being from America?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes. The taller one, 191 or 192 centimetres, said that he was from Belgrade, Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The one that identified himself as being from the United States, can I ask you to give a physical description of him?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: He was somewhere 180 or 182 centimetres tall, black hair, short. Some 30-odd years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was that person able to speak Serbian?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, but with quite a heavy accent, an American accent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to describe the physical build of the person who identified himself as American?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Thin. Quite thin. He wasn't bulky. Thin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did one of these two men do most of the talking or did they talk approximately the same amount each?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: No. The one from America was leading the conversation with me, and he took notes and he told me how I should testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you now to describe what happened after these two people arrived in the house of MLD-10?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: She went with them into that room. She talked there for 10 minutes, and then I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Alarid is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness apologized for mentioning the witness's name, MLD-10 came out in B/C/S. It didn't make the transcript, but it is recorded. So we need the video or audio redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's being redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, where were you at the time that MLD-10 was meeting with these two lawyers?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I was seated with MLD-10's husband in the living-room. In the living-room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you able to tell where they went to have this discussion?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. Into the adjoining room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did there come a time when they returned to the room that you were in?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: No. Well, MLD-10 did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened when MLD-10 came out of that room?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Then I went to that other room. We got acquainted and we started our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there anyone else in the room besides yourself and these two men?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: No, the three of us only.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As precisely as you are able to do, can I ask you to recount what was said in that room.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Since I already had read the letter from Mr. Lukic, Milan Lukic, I knew what this was all about. They offered me the same thing and they told me, Milan is going to give you everything that you would need in your life. I responded, What is everything in life exactly? And they replied, Everything. And said, Well, if I die tomorrow, I would have nothing of that. And they said, Well, in precise terms, 100.000 Euro. I was silent for awhile after that. I was thinking, looking at them. And then finally I said, 100.000 Euro? And he responded, Yes, just to confirm what I had given in the previous statement so that I can confirm what had already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Which of the two spoke to you about the 100.000 Euros?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: The one from America.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did they tell you what you needed to do in order to get that 100.000 Euros?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, they did. I was supposed to go and confirm -- to go to The Hague to defend Milan Lukic, and to confirm that Hamdija Vilic, military commander of Muslim forces, on the 12th of June, 1992, encircled a military column of Serbian soldiers, killed three Serb officers, and kept Milan and his unit, his troops, for three days and three nights in encirclement in the forest next to the village of Kopito.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did you respond or what did you say in response to their proposal?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I said that I did not remember that ever anyone from the Serb -- on the part of the Serb forces or the Muslim forces was ever in a forest in a village being encircled, and that they could not reach the place where their unit, their troops had been stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you accept their proposal?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: No. No, I did not accept their proposal. I said that this wasn't true, and that I would not most probably be testifying for the benefit of Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did they ever discuss your wife and children?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a note whether there was any response when he did not accept their proposal and said it wasn't true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour is asking -- Judge Robinson is asking, did they make any response to you when you told them you were not interested in their proposal?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: No. I told them about the truth about Milan setting my family to fire in that house, but they did not like the answer. They did not continue or persist with their desire for me to testify in this way. But they did not like my proposals because they said this would not be beneficial to him. The only beneficial testimony for him would be what they had proposed to me, and -- but I could not accept that even for 100.000 millions of Euros.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Once you declined their proposal, did you feel as though any pressure was put on you to change your mind?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: No, no, they did not apply any pressure. They simply said, We will be in touch. The one from Belgrade, the alleged lawyer, he said to the guy from America, You will get to The Hague, you will see Milan Lukic, and tell him and relate the course of that conversation to him. In the meantime, we started saying our good-byes, Adieu, sir. I demanded for my taxi expenses to be reimbursed because that had been our understanding. The bloke from America said to the guy from Belgrade, How much is that? I said taxi from Sarajevo to Zavidovici was 250 Euro. My per diem would be 50 Euro, that would be 300 Euro. The one from America said to the Belgrade guy, Give him the money. He opened the suitcase, it was a laptop-sized case. It was full of Euros, Euro notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Sir --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: We said good-bye to each other --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before we go any further, can I ask you to -- a few specific questions about this proposal. Were you a military commander in the Federation army in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: No. I was never such a commander throughout the period between 1992 and 1996. I was a plain soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In June of 1992, were you ever engaged in any kind of activity that might be considered of a military nature in the area of Kopito?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During this time that you were in MLD-10's home, were you aware that she had spoken to anyone on a telephone?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I was. On the 22nd of June, between 4.00 -- well, around 4.00 p.m., she received at least three phone calls from The Hague, from Milan Lukic. She was crying saying, "Brother, may god bring you luck. I don't know what else to wish you." That is what she said in front of me. There were two or three calls from The Hague by Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to summarize for the Chamber, how it was that you came to provide this information to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I was in Vogosca in the bar with some friends of mine. There was a friend, a comrade of someone who had been in The Hague, I don't know if I can mention the name. In any case, Ferid said that Milan Lukic had said that he had offered me money. This person, Ferid, called me and asked me if he was allowed to give my phone number to The Hague Prosecutor's Office, and whether I would be willing to go to The Hague to testify about this. I told him I would with pleasure, and here I am. Ferid then placed a call, and a few days later, I received a phone call from the OTP. A lady introduced herself, I cannot recall her name right now, and asked me if I would be willing to meet with a Prosecutor in Sarajevo. I said that I would. I don't know who the Prosecutor concerned was, but in any case, we met in Sarajevo. I provided a statement, much as I did here. And that would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you recall the date when this person spoke to you in the bar, and in particular, I want to find out what was the interval of time between the time when you spoke with the two lawyers and that particular time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps five to ten days or so. I'm not really sure. I didn't keep any records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, I'm going to ask you to look at an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's ERN 05450789. It's a still from P54, the 360 programme. I'd ask that just one image in its largest capacity be displayed for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise what this photograph depicts?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you be able to identify your brother's house on this photograph, if called upon to do so?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'd ask you to place your initials somewhere along the bottom edge of the image so we know that it's you that has made the markings. And I'd ask you to circle your brother's house where you've testified your wife and children were staying.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could I ask to you put an A next to that circle so we know that's what it indicates.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions of this witness. I'm sorry, Your Honour, I forgot to formally tender the document. Thank you for the suggestive looks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number P195.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you, Witness, in the five to ten days between the time that you met the two lawyers and the time when you met somebody in the bar, what was going through your mind in relation to this entire transaction? Did you form any view about this transaction, the proposal that was made to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I did. Of course even to this day I think about it. Had I accepted Milan Lukic's attorney's proposal, it would have been as if selling out my wife, my children, my brother, my neighbours, and everyone else in exchange for money. I probably would not be able to live with such a thing for a long time. This way, it is easier for me to live, although I don't have the money. At least I can tell the Bench what means they use which are completely wrong. They are ready to pay money to be acquitted, although they had done what they were accused of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you ever consider reporting the matter to the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. I did talk to some people senior to me, who are better educated, although I have a certain amount of education myself. I finished high school, a good one. In any case, I simply did not want to consent to such offers. I was thinking of forwarding that information to the Bosnian Prosecutor's Office. However, the way things went seemed better to me than me reporting it to the police or anyone else down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Considering the timing of the break, Your Honour, it's only 5 minutes away, could we take the break and then just start fresh?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vilic.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: My name is Jason Alarid and I'm the attorney for Milan Lukic. I'd like to ask you a few questions about your testimony. Okay?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak up and move closer to the microphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, the interpreter is having difficulty hearing you. Please come forward a little and speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the first thing that I'd like to do is on behalf of my client, he asked me to give my condolences for you and your family, and the family members that you lost during the war.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And beyond that, I'd like to ask going back before you ever knew about the Milan Lukic request for your testimony, had you heard anything about this case, just in the news, the media things like that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: About Milan's case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had. I was following it on Bosnian TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And before Milan Lukic's arrest and being able to follow it on TV, did you follow the earlier case, Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when your -- would it be fair to say that when your cousin contacted you, that you might be going to testify or asked to testify in this case, you were told that it was about the time period in mid-June; correct, 1992 being?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, would your cousin have had an understanding that you were a soldier in the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And according to your earlier testimony, and it may be slightly different from your statement you gave in this case, but it's my understanding that you formally joined the Bosnian military about June 20th of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And why do you consider June 20th the day you formally joined the military?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Because that's when I joined the Bosnian military.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And to formally do that, how did you do that? Was there a swearing-in ceremony? Did you take an oath? What happened to formally join the military?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: There were no ceremonies. It was a state of war. There were no oaths either. I simply approached them and joined the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Where did you approach them?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: In Medjedja.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How did you get to Medjedja?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Through the forest. At night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you arrive in Medjedja on the 20th or later?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I arrived there before that, and spent some three days there before joining the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so isn't it true that three days earlier you were in the area of Kopito, on that journey?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, the war had been going on, or the state of war had been going on since early April; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I believe the anniversary for the start is about the April 6th or April 5th, depending on who you talk to, is that true, in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, around that date. On the 6th the Uzice Corps arrived. Once they left, paramilitary units remained. One of those were the White Eagles where Milan was at first. Then he organised a unit of his own, Osvetnici, the Avengers. He was in command of that unit doing whatever he wanted. As the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: -- accused Vasiljevic said --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Where did you read this?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: On TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. So what you are reciting is not based on your personal knowledge but from what you got from television; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I saw Vasiljevic personally. I saw him speak. I heard what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the -- your own experience with the war, when were you when the Uzice Corps came to town?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I was in Prelovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when did you formally go into hiding, no longer coming out for fear of being taken captive or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: It was sometime in June. I came to Bikavac in my brother's house and I started hiding in the forest immediately. I only came there at night, and sometimes during the day when we were certain that there was no danger. However, there was always a possibility of being caught by Milan or some others who were with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true that there were hundreds of Serbian soldiers in the Visegrad area? That the Uzice Corps had left a large number of soldiers there in Visegrad along with their weapons and military armaments?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: While the Uzice Corps was there, things were fine. Once they left, I'm not saying no one remained, but there were paramilitaries. They called them volunteers. Some of them must have remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And during the time the Uzice Corps were there, the Muslim population was disarmed; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that left them helpless for the volunteers that stayed behind; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Milan Lukic's volunteers and Milan himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But the fact is, is you testified that you didn't see Milan Lukic before the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I had seen him before the war and during the war at Bikavac in my brother's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the fact of the matter is, though, you did not before -- you don't know when Milan Lukic arrived in town, do you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I don't know precisely. I can't tell you the exact date, but he must have arrived along with his pals at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when you say "he must have," you are guessing, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't see him then because the war was underway already, and it was good for me that I didn't see him, otherwise, he would have arrested and killed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true that at the time that the aggression started from the Serbians, there were Muslims that took up arms, took to the forests and put up a resistance; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Well, people were of course fleeing to the woods, they were afraid. They were afraid of murders, but for the most part they were only armed with hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so those people, those people, they were still acting as resistance, as soldiers against the Serb aggression; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems to me if Mr. Alarid. At the beginning of my examination, rose to complain that I might be going too broad, it seems unfair now at this stage that he gives himself latitude he wouldn't accord me. It seems that his questions should be limited to the direct examination which was directly related to the alibi evidence that this man gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to ask Mr. Alarid to explain to us the relevance of all of this in relation to this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, one, Your Honour, is I think it's fair to put to the witness his involvement with the military right as the war started and when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why is it? Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's still my position, at least we had information that he was part of a group that had this Serb detachment cut off where Commander Tripkovic was killed and it's documented. So that was a -- it was a -- we'll call it a skirmish in the area, so given the fact of that from an opportunity and position this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And even if that is so, it's not clear to me how it becomes relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Because if he is really in Kopito, Your Honour -- and we are having the conversation with the witness present which is problematic, but you are asking me to explain my cross-examination of the witness in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is wrong with that? That is pretty standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, no. Speaking objections in front of the witness are not standard, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. We do that here, and don't tell me about your national jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, no. It's just our conversation can contaminate the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Anything I say he can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You just continue. Just continue --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- and leave this topic very quickly. Move on to another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so isn't it true that members in the -- of the local community were joining that resistance, were they not?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: In the village of Kopito there was never a military column that had been cut off or intercepted, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That's what is important, sir, because if you are not participating in it, how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I know it from others. There were no attacks of -- or columns being intercepted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sir, if we know the date that Commander Tripkovic was killed, clearly there was an attack that day. And so tell me what you know about that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it so clear? I mean, there are mines used in war, we have heard no evidence about how this person by the name of Tripkovic died, whether it was a mine or an attack. So it's not so clear that there must have been an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That kind of speaking objection, Your Honours, is tantamount to leading the witness. It really is. And that's -- I understand the point of different policies and procedures but that is what I'm talking about. If you are allowed to make that kind of speaking objection in front of the witness, he is privy to our argument and nuance, and it really gives the witness really a nuance of where to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, the main reason why sometimes witnesses are asked to leave the court in the common law system is because there is a -- the jury may be contaminated. And sometimes jurors are asked to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: True, true, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have any jury here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I am more worried about the witness, Your Honour. THE COURT: We are professional judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That's true, I'm not worried about you, Your Honour. I'm worried about the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's no problem with the witness. I'm worried about your evidence and where it is leading. I don't see it leading anywhere. So please get to the point, if there is one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you hear about Tripkovic being killed, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I mean, the witness is enjoying our discourse, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think it's provocative to the witness and how does Mr. Alarid know whether the witness is enjoying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's an aside. Let's leave that, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, then let the record reflect the witness is chuckling during Your Honour's and my conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've had enough of that. Get on with the questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What did you hear about Tripkovic's death, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear about him. I only know what Milan wrote in his letter, that there were three Serb officers who were killed at Kopito. What I claim is that there was not an attack or an interception of any Serb forces at Kopito ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, for reference, sir, the attack that I'm referring to occurred at Gornja Lijeska which is 2 kilometres from Kopito?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Lauske? Never heard of that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You've never heard of that place. Now, but you did say that you had heard that there was nothing there because you heard it from other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But even that particular time, sir, you didn't know it was Milan Lukic, you were told by someone else; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, as if I did not know Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic and could not tell those two apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sir, we are talking about Milan Lukic, and I'm asking you before the time in Bikavac, when was the last time you saw him so maybe you could have a reference point of identifying him. Can you think back and tell me when the time before the war, when was the last time you saw this Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Was he a man or a boy?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Well, younger and quite thinner than he is right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I'm talking before the war. How old was he the last time --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes. How old was he the last time?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: How could I know what age he was? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Because you said you knew him well from before the war, so I'm trying to figure out how you knew him well.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: How could I not know him? I visited those villages, my aunt lived in his village. I used to see him around town on buses. I don't know and how could I know his age. I wasn't the -- working as a registrar when he was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No, but most times you can look at somebody and kind of at least tell in a range of how old they are. And you may not be able to tell their birthday but you might know whether they are a teenager or a young adult or a small boy. And I'm asking you when is the last time you saw him whether up in the village or on the bus or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall that. Most probably he wasn't a boy or a child, he was a lad of some 25, 30 years of age, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can we have ERN 06428393 placed on the screen, please. Maybe the better way to do it is, 2D04-0537.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, sir, while we are waiting for that to come on the screen, would it be fair to say then before 1992, the Milan Lukic you are talking about was 25 to 30 years old?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: How could I know? Approximately. Well, you are forcing me to pinpoint his age and I just said that I could not really know his age.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And we could go to the last page, please. It would be the last page of the English. It's a photo lineup. If we could just make that the full page, probably, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true, sir, that you were shown this photo lineup before?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you were asked if you recognised anyone, and you recognised someone to be Milan Lukic, number 3; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I said I wasn't certain. Those are pictures not of high quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you specifically indicated that number 8 looks like Sredoje Lukic; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Something like that, but I also stated that I wasn't certain because the photos were not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And otherwise, you didn't recognise anyone else in this photo spread; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: As you can see for yourself, they almost look the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: All right. I have no further use of this exhibit. We would tender 2D040537 into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: It's the statement of this witness who was shown a photospread and he identified someone who looked like Milan, looked like Sredoje and no one else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D91, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when you had the meeting with these two lawyers, how long total did you talk with them, sit with them, interact with them at this house?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: 30, 40 minutes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the one that you called the American lawyer, you indicated that he spoke Serbian, but with a strong accent?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And can you tell me what kind of accent?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I don't know. The Rs were characteristic. He spoke in a manner of a foreigner speaking Bosnian or Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, was he fluent or did he have trouble with words?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: He pronounced those words quite well, but not exactly in a way that you could get the meaning straightaway. And he would mix certain words up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Alarid and Mr. Groome. The information that I requested of the registry has been provided, and I'll ask the court deputy to make it available to the parties. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when you said that he mixed certain words up, was that because he was not comfortable or fluent in the language?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Most probably this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did it seem like Serbian was a second language and not a born language?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you tell whether or not an accent is from Belgrade or Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Approximately, yes. The Belgrade accent would be like "Lepo" and similar words would be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did the one that posed as an American have any kind of accent that you would be able to recognise other than it was maybe a second language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did he say posed as an American?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, called -- I think called him. I don't know which way you want to look at it, Judge. I think it was -- I used that term, so that's a loaded word, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think you should rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I mean, called himself an American?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's normal that this would be a second or foreign language, the Serbian or Bosnian, because he was taught in English over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you have any discussions about his background or where he was from or how he had learned Serbian?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true that Gornja Lijeska is 2 kilometres from Kopito?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: What kind of Lijoska?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Gornja Lijeska.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Ah, Lijeska. Gornja Lijeska, I don't know what is the exact distance in kilometres. First you get to Gornja Lijeska then Kopito, and then further towards Rogatica there are some other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when you journeyed to this meeting, you indicated that you were told to take the most expensive cab you could; is that true?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, are there other ways to get from Sarajevo to Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Not to Visegrad. Why Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What I'm just saying is you took a cab where you went. I'm sorry if it wasn't Visegrad, but you took a cab. How many kilometres did you take a cab?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo to Zenica is 80 kilometres, and then 70 kilometres which would add up to 160, 170 kilometres in one direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true you could have taken a bus or made alternative arrangements?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Well, I took my own car.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, if you took your own car, then why do we need a cab reimbursement for you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Because they had told me that they would pay for a cab.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So you lied to the attorneys and told them that you had taken a cab instead of taking your own car?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Is this prohibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You didn't take a cab; right?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I took my vehicle which I own.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you were told before your meeting that you were going to be reimbursed for your travel expenses; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you took that to mean that you could demand 250 Euros for a cab ride that you didn't take; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Why wouldn't I charge them for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, because you didn't have to pay -- you only had to pay for your gas; correct? You didn't have to pay a cab driver for the use of his cab.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I did -- there was depreciation for the car registration, road toll, motor oil, tire wear, everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And also for his time, if you want to get into the economics of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I believe that was 50 Euros for the time. 50 Euros for 40 minutes. But we are more concerned about the veracity of the statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I told you the truth that I did take my own car.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so then also isn't it true that you are the one that demanded 100.000 Euros from Milan Lukic to tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: No, never. This is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, don't you think it's funny -- well, one is, is what you were requested to say didn't involve you actually seeing Milan Lukic; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Well, of course I would have seen him if I had come here to testify on his -- to his benefit, but I did see him right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. That's something that has been passing through my mind. When you went to the meeting with the lawyers, what exactly did they say to you? What is it that they wanted you to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, they wanted to tell me to -- me to tell you this, that my name was Hamdija Vilic and that I commanded Muslim forces. Then that I cut a military convoy in half at Kopito, killing three officers and keeping Milan Lukic and his soldiers, that is to say, his units for three days and nights in encirclement, during which time he could not have been in Visegrad because he is probably charged with something that happened during the three days. They didn't want to tell me what. I refused that and I said that such a convoy was never cut in half in that place, and that no Serb soldiers or Muslim soldiers, for that matter, were in any encirclement. Not even for an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. So let me confirm, the statement that they wanted you to make did involve saying something about Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That it was done by the Uzice or Valjevo Corps and the White Eagles, and that Milan Lukic did not do that and that he never had any unit of his. I told them this: You were in Belgrade and you were in America, and now you are telling me what happened while I was in the environs of Visegrad, about what Milan had at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm still not clear, but it's important what the Judge asked you. Isn't it true that they did not ask you to commit that you actually saw Milan Lukic, that you could see him and recognise him, merely that you were involved in a battle of which Milan Lukic now claims to have partaked [sic] in on the other side; correct.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. I can try to clarify something though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you this: The kind of fighting that would have been up there would have been guerilla warfare; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: One could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Members of the army hiding and ambushing and keeping other people in another army pinned down; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Only with stones and hoes, how could we ambush someone?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in guerilla warfare, the terrain and the trees and things are used as cover so people can't see each other well enough to shoot each other; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Well, normally if I saw someone, I would kill him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just like you did in that bar with that grenade; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: This is not the subject matter here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, it is because the Prosecutor brought up your felony criminal conviction for murder, and so we need to talk about that before I let you go. And so you were willing to kill people on sight if need be; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Only in self-defence. And I killed a Muslim person, not a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this was you using a grenade or a bomb in a bar fight; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: You shouldn't be concerned with that. I served my sentence for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But it shows you were a fighter and not afraid of violence, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Well, killing someone doesn't necessarily mean that you are a fighter. You can only be a coward.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you have a never been a coward; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I might have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you were willing to fight as early as you could in the conflict, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: What conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I had to defend.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, do you know who Ibro Kabaklija?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: The late.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you knew him, yes, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: He used to work with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And he also led fighters in the area around Visegrad, did he not?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And his brother Nermin, he also was a fighter with him?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: A plain fighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And Jamak Esad?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I don't know that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How about Jamak?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: A plain fighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And these gentleman killed Nenad Markovic near Kopito in June, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA VILIC
utterances.text: I don't know when Markovic was killed and by whom. I'm not interested in that and I don't think I need to answer such questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, isn't it true, though, that you have been placed fighting with Ibro's group?
